definition: Reciprocal means given, felt, or done in return — shared equally in both directions by both sides.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word reciprocal. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know reciprocal should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The two nations signed a reciprocal trade agreement, each cutting taxes on the other's goods.
A shared interest just means two people like the same thing; a reciprocal bond means each one actively gives something back to the other.
A reciprocal partnership trades favors back and forth, but an interdependent one goes further — neither side could function alone.

Mutual means shared or felt by both parties — mutual respect, a mutual friend — and it describes the state of having something in common. Reciprocal is more active: each side actually gives something and gets something back, a flow of exchange rather than a shared possession.

Two-way is the plain, practical word for anything that carries traffic in both directions — a two-way street, a two-way mirror — and it is the fixed phrase for equipment that sends and receives. Reciprocal belongs to relationships and arrangements between people: favors, trust, and agreements given and returned.

Returned describes a single answered act — a returned favor, returned affection: someone gave, and the other gave back once. Reciprocal describes the standing pattern in which giving flows both ways as a matter of course, not just one repaid instance.

Reciprocal describes an arrangement, feeling, or action that flows equally in both directions: reciprocal trust, a reciprocal favor, a reciprocal agreement.
Cross-reference: the related verb form, reciprocate ('to give something in return'), names the action itself — reciprocal is the adjective that describes the two-way relationship itself.
If only one side gives, the relationship is one-way, not reciprocal.

When the flood closed Ridgeview High's gymnasium, the school across town offered its courts for the season.
Nobody at the time called it anything but a favor.
But the arrangement that grew out of that winter became genuinely reciprocal.
Ridgeview hosts the other school's swim team every fall, since it has the only indoor pool in the county; the other school lends its stage and lighting rig each spring for Ridgeview's musical.
The exchange now runs on a schedule, written into each school's calendar, and neither side keeps score.
Ask either principal and you get the same answer: what began as one kindness has settled into a steady trade of them.
